subject: Biology
title: ATP: The Energy Currency
description: A micro-lesson that makes ATP: The Energy Currency usable.

hook.text: ATP is a tiny molecule that powers almost every process in every living cell.

buildup.text: When ATP loses a phosphate group, it releases energy. The cell uses that burst to do work.

discovery.text: You produce roughly your own body weight in ATP every single day, recycling it constantly.

twist.text: ATP lasts only seconds before it's broken down and rebuilt. Your body never stockpiles it.

climax.text: From thinking to blinking, from dividing to digesting—ATP fuels all of it.

punchline.text: One molecule runs the whole show.

quiz.question: How much ATP does the human body produce daily?

details.summary: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the universal energy currency of all living cells. When its high-energy phosphate bond is broken, it releases energy that powers virtually every cellular process from muscle contraction to DNA replication to active transport.
details.whyItMatters: Every living organism runs on ATP. The human body produces and consumes roughly its own weight in ATP every day, making it the single most important molecule for sustaining cellular life and function.
takeaways: ATP stores energy in its phosphate bonds and releases it when broken
The body produces roughly its own weight in ATP daily through recycling
ATP powers muscle contraction, nerve signaling, and biosynthesis

faq.question: How does ATP release energy?
faq.answer: When the terminal phosphate bond is hydrolyzed by enzymes, ATP becomes ADP plus a free phosphate group, releasing energy that is coupled to cellular work. ADP is then recycled back to ATP in mitochondria, creating a continuous energy cycle.

faq.question: Why is ATP called the energy currency?
faq.answer: Just as currency is a universal medium of exchange in economics, ATP is the universal medium of energy transfer in cells. Energy from food is converted to ATP, which then spends that energy on whatever the cell needs, from movement to growth.
